beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The filesystem is the meeting room.
beats.got: Agents hand work to each other through shared files, a bit like a shared drive between colleagues.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: Nothing new. There is homework, and I don't know what my "challenge memory" is yet.

beats.trigger: **Analyze** handoff failures: hidden conflicts, clashing dialects, beige averaging
beats.got: I'll build agents that search and agents that decide. The word "dialect" is used before I know what it means.

beats.trigger: Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.
beats.got: Six agents in two groups, three to find and three to judge. It's concrete, but nothing yet about who in my organisation does this work.

beats.trigger: The agent writes the message first and sends only after approval.
beats.got: An agent can act in another system, but only with a human approval gate. That is something I can say to my DPO and the works council.

beats.trigger: Ask the agent to name the sharpest decision it blocks, the call you'd stay late to make
beats.got: The agent can push me from a topic to the one decision that matters, which is a useful habit for a leadership team too.

beats.trigger: Three retrievers fetch raw material on your challenge into `sources/`; a fourth session curates it into `memory/`.
beats.got: Four sessions open at once, with a lot of files and folders. I can do it, but I can't see who owns this afterwards, and Confluence and OneDrive may hold employee data.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if the answer is right. That is expected. Name the doubt; don't fix it here.
beats.got: The synthesis can sound confident without being verified, and I'm told to carry that doubt openly. I appreciate the honesty.

beats.trigger: Two ways to split an agent: three retrievers in separate windows, three stances inside one session.
beats.got: There are two ways to split agents: separate sessions, or helpers inside one session.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: The unit is a recurring workflow, not a role or a person. That sounds like how I'd map HR processes, and it finally gives me something to take to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: The default is one agent, and splitting has to be justified. This is understated advice, which I like.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Different access is a legitimate reason to split. That is a privacy and governance argument, not just a technical one, and I can use it.

beats.trigger: More input does not fix a beige answer.
beats.got: More agents doesn't mean a better answer. It adds noise and cost.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.
beats.got: Without a framework the synthesis averages the views. With one it has to choose, much like a leadership team needs a decision rule.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: Before building a multi-agent setup, ask whether one prompt would do the same job. That's a good gate question.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).** Pick this for quick parallel thinking with a bounded return.
beats.got: Sessions for agents that stay alive, helpers for in-and-out jobs. I've heard both terms but couldn't explain the difference to someone else yet.

beats.trigger: One agent can call another for a different stance, source zone, or working style.

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.
beats.got: Errors happen at handoffs, and a silent choice between two numbers can reach a decision. It's the same risk as a game of telephone between teams.

beats.trigger: If one well-prompted agent does the job, write that prompt.
beats.got: nothing new. It repeats the earlier slides.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail in a few recognisable ways, and "confident right before a failed handoff" is the one that worries me.

beats.trigger: Prompt your stuck system to diagnose whether the bug lives in the sources, the processing, or the boundary between agents.
beats.got: I can ask the agent to find where its own work went wrong before I try to fix anything.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agents bring new risks on top of normal security, like prompt injection. It confirms I need the DPO and the works council involved. The jargon is heavy, though.

beats.got: An agent has whatever access its connections give it, so I should ask what the worst case is before I connect HR data.

take_homes: Split into several agents only when they need different access, a different dialect or a different stance. Otherwise one good prompt is better. The access test is a privacy argument I can take to my DPO.
A synthesis can sound confident without being checked, and handoffs between agents are where facts get lost or silently dropped. A human gate (propose, not do) is how to keep it safe.
A framework (diagnosis, policy, actions) forces the synthesizer to choose instead of averaging. I could use the same discipline on the leadership team's headcount question.

monday.move: Nothing with agents yet. I'd ask my DPO and the works council contact what employee data may go into an AI tool. Then I'd pick one recurring HR workflow, probably the weekly people-metrics summary, and ask whether one agent would do.
monday.who: Me, my DPO, and one HR business partner
monday.when: Early next week, before I touch any employee data
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO or works council says employee data cannot go into the tool, I stop and use only non-personal data.
monday.blocker: The works council and DPO have not been asked yet, and I don't know yet who would own the agent after me.

misconception.why: The module never talks about roles or headcount. It is about how to split agents. The workflow-as-unit and human-gate slides make me think about who owns the work, but nothing shows me which roles go or don't, so I still expect headcount to be the first question in the leadership team.

one_line: Useful rule of thumb for when to use several agents and when not to, and honest about not knowing if the answer is true, but it never says what any of it means for the people doing the work.
